origin_region: Central highlands · Kirinyaga, Nyeri and Nandi
processing: Hand-plucked buds and young leaf withered slowly in shade for a day or more and dried gently without rolling; oxidation is incidental. A small speciality line at orthodox-capable factories.
harvest_season: Year-round in small pluckings; the dry seasons give the plumpest buds.
appearance_dry: Silvery-downy buds, slightly darker and chunkier than Fujian Silver Needle.
taste_profile: Soft honey and hay with a melon-like sweetness and a fuller, rounder body than Chinese white teas; almost no astringency.

brewing.notes: Five minutes or more at 80 °C; re-steeps two or three times without turning bitter.

vintage_note: Sold in small lots by factory and plucking date through speciality importers and Kenyan direct-trade brands, priced well above the country's black teas because of the hand-picking. Drink within a year or two; not an ageing tea.
description:
Kenyan white tea is a small speciality line from the central highlands: downy buds and young leaf from the same clonal bushes that supply the CTC factories, withered slowly and dried without rolling. It has existed for only a couple of decades, made by a few orthodox-capable factories and smallholder groups in Kirinyaga, Nyeri and Nandi for direct-trade and speciality buyers.

Buds are plucked by hand, which in a country built on fast machine-grade plucking is itself unusual, then withered in shade for a day or more and dried gently; there is no rolling and only incidental oxidation. The equatorial climate means it can be made year-round, with the plumpest buds in the dry seasons.

The cup is pale gold and tastes of honey and hay with a melon-like sweetness and a fuller, rounder body than Chinese white teas, with almost no astringency. Brew it at around 80 °C for five minutes or more and re-steep two or three times.

It is sold in small lots by factory and plucking date through speciality importers and Kenyan direct-trade brands, priced well above the country's black teas because of the hand-picking. Drink it within a year or two.

Worth a try as a comparison with Fujian or Darjeeling white teas: same method, very different leaf.
sources_note: Kenyan white tea is a small niche; the producing areas and 'couple of decades' history are from memory and worth a check.
